sources_considered.why: The official November 2023 supercomputer ranking gives machine floating point throughput.
Human-versus-GPT-4 comparison on a flexible abstraction benchmark from November 2023.
NeurIPS 2023 study of GPT-4's autonomous planning success.

receipt.public_excerpt: Frontier leads the pack with an HPL score of 1.194 EFlop/s – unchanged from the June 2023 list.

evidence_items.explanation: The top machine sustained about 1.2 quintillion floating point operations per second on the Linpack benchmark, vastly beyond any human rate. This supports 'light years ahead' on floating point arithmetic.

evidence_items.locator: Section 3 (Previous Evaluation of LLMs using the ConceptARC Benchmark)

receipt.public_excerpt: the overall accuracy of humans was 91%, compared to the first-place Kaggle program’s accuracy of 52%, and GPT-4’s accuracy of 25% (using temperature 0.5).

evidence_items.explanation: On tasks that test applying abstract concepts flexibly to new cases, both the best program and GPT-4 were well below humans in 2023. This supports 'way behind' on cognitive flexibility.

receipt.public_excerpt: However, GPT-4’s performance remains well below the high performance of humans, supporting the conclusion that, even with more informative prompting, the system lacks basic abstract reasoning abilities tested by this corpus.

evidence_items.explanation: Even with better prompting, GPT-4 reached only 33% in November 2023, so the flexibility gap was not an artefact of weak prompting.

receipt.public_excerpt: Our findings reveal that LLMs' ability to generate executable plans autonomously is rather limited, with the best model (GPT-4) having an average success rate of ~12% across the domains.

evidence_items.explanation: The best LLM in 2023 produced valid plans only about 12% of the time on standard planning domains. This supports 'way behind' on planning. The paper also finds better results when external planners and verifiers are added.

unresolved_gaps: No direct human baseline was found for the planning benchmark. 'Way behind humans' on planning is inferred from the low absolute success on commonsense planning tasks.

Classical symbolic planners solve these planning domains well, so 'machines' in the broad sense are not uniformly behind on planning. The claim is read as being about flexible planning in unusual situations.
